opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm pretty humble about predicting the next major advance, because if you'd asked most of us a few years ago, very few would have called exactly how quickly things would move or which directions would matter most. So rather than trying to pick the one breakthrough, I think about it more as watching a few signals.

One is where people are hitting walls today. When you work with customers deploying these systems, you see very concretely where the technology falls short: reliability, grounding in real data, handling long and complex tasks, knowing when it doesn't know something. Those pain points tend to be where a lot of energy goes, and where meaningful progress shows up next.

Another is looking at what's working in research but isn't yet practical. Often the next "big advance" from a user's perspective is something that's existed in some form for a while and finally became efficient, cheap, or robust enough to use at scale. So a lot of the change isn't one magical leap. It's many pieces maturing at once and suddenly being usable together.

And from my vantage point, working on responsible AI, I also think about what has to be true for these advances to be adopted. A capability that's impressive in a demo but that you can't measure, test, or put guardrails around won't have the same impact as one that people can trust. So I watch the tooling around evaluation, safety, and transparency as closely as the raw capabilities, because that's often what determines whether something becomes a real advance in the world or stays a research curiosity.

So I don't try to predict the exact headline. I try to stay close to the problems, stay close to the research, and build the practices that let us move quickly and responsibly whatever comes next.

r001.rationale: The response says past advances and their directions were hard to predict, but does not attribute this to people reverting to linear expectations between major releases.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-5 or whether it will eliminate prompt engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've mostly given up on trying to predict the specific next advance, because every time I've tried, I've been wrong about the what and roughly right about the shape. So I think about it less as "what's the next model capability" and more as "where is the friction right now, and what would it take to remove it."

If you look back, each of the big jumps happened where there was a gap between what people wanted to do and what the technology let them do in practice. We had models that could generate text, and the friction was that you couldn't steer them, so instruction tuning and RLHF were the advance. Then the friction was that they didn't know anything about your data, so retrieval became the thing. Now the friction is that they can't reliably act over long horizons, so a lot of energy is going into agents, tool use, and the evaluation and safety infrastructure to make that trustworthy.

So my heuristic is: watch what people are doing awkwardly. When you see a lot of engineers building elaborate scaffolding around a model to get a behavior, that scaffolding is a prediction. Either the model will absorb it, or the tooling around it will mature until it disappears.

The other thing I'd say, coming from the responsible AI side, is that the advances that actually matter in the world are rarely just capability advances. The thing that made generative AI usable at scale wasn't only that the models got better, it was that we figured out how to ground them, test them, and put guardrails around them so an enterprise could actually ship. I'd expect the next major advance to have that same character. It'll be partly a research breakthrough and partly a maturity breakthrough, and the second half is the part people tend to underestimate.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s really hard to predict the next major advance. You can see directions where there’s a lot of promise, but there’s a difference between showing that something is possible and getting it to work reliably enough that people can use it.

So I tend to think about what’s holding us back today. Where do these models struggle? Where do people have to do a lot of work to get a useful result? An advance might be a new capability, but it might also be making an existing capability much more reliable or accessible. That can have a big impact, even if it doesn’t look like a dramatic breakthrough on a benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s really hard to predict the next major advance. There are so many things moving at once—the models themselves, how we train them, and how people use them. And a capability that looks incremental in a research setting can become a big deal when somebody finds the right application for it.

So I tend to think less about predicting a single breakthrough and more about what’s keeping these systems from being useful today. Can we make them more reliable? Can we give people better ways to guide them and evaluate their outputs? Progress on those questions could have a huge impact, even if it doesn’t look like a dramatic new model capability.
